source: Cornell Cooperative Extension NYS IPM Small Fruit Program / University of Minnesota Extension Strawberry Disease Guidelines
title: Strawberry Leaf Scorch (Diplocarpon earlianum, anamorph Marssonina fragariae)
content: Strawberry leaf scorch is the most common, widely distributed, and economically important foliar disease of cultivated strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa Duch.) worldwide in cool-temperate, humid, and maritime production regions with frequent spring and summer rainfall. The causal organism is the hemibiotrophic ascomycete fungus Diplocarpon earlianum (Ellis & Everh.) F.A. Wolf (class Leotiomycetes, order Helotiales, family Drepanopezizaceae; asexual anamorphic stage: Marssonina fragariae (Lib.) Magnus, formerly known as Marssonina potentillae f. fragariae). Leaf scorch occurs in all major strawberry-producing states and provinces of the United States and Canada (particularly severe in the northeastern US, Great Lakes region, Pacific Northwest, and the Canadian Maritimes), northern, western, and central Europe, the United Kingdom, southern Chile and Argentina, New Zealand, southeastern Australia, northern Japan, and the cool high-altitude regions of western North America and East Africa. While leaf scorch rarely kills outright infected strawberry plants, severe repeated annual infections reduce healthy photosynthetic leaf area by 30-70%, cause premature leaf necrosis and defoliation 4-6 weeks before the normal end of the growing season, reduce plant vigor and runner production for propagation nurseries, decrease winter survival of strawberry crowns by 20-40% due to reduced carbohydrate reserves, reduce fruit size and soluble solids (sugar) content of harvested fruit, and increase fruit sunscald losses due to premature loss of the protective leaf canopy. Total annual fruit yield losses of 15-35% are documented on susceptible strawberry cultivars in years with extended cool, wet, rainy spring and early summer conditions. D. earlianum is specialized to the genus Fragaria and does not infect any other genus of plants; it naturally infects cultivated F. x ananassa, the wild diploid woodland strawberry F. vesca L., the wild North American octoploid F. virginiana Mill. and F. chiloensis (L.) Mill., and some other wild Fragaria species. The first symptoms of strawberry leaf scorch appear on the upper surfaces of the oldest (outermost), lowest-positioned basal leaflets approximately 2-4 weeks after new spring growth resumes, or 3-6 weeks after transplanting plug transplants into new fields. Initial symptoms are tiny (0.5-1 mm), circular, dark purple to reddish-brown necrotic spots scattered randomly across the upper (adaxial) leaflet surface, not associated with veins or leaf margins. As the season progresses and the pathogen undergoes repeated secondary cycles, individual spots enlarge to 1-5 mm in diameter, become circular to slightly angular, develop a distinct dark brown to deep purple or reddish-brown (maroon) color, and are typically surrounded by a narrow, bright yellow chlorotic halo when held up against transmitted sunlight. The diagnostic feature that distinguishes leaf scorch from the other major strawberry foliar disease (leaf spot = Mycosphaerella fragariae, 'white spot' / 'bird's eye spot') is that leaf scorch lesions remain uniformly dark purple/reddish-brown throughout the lesion center at maturity and never develop the characteristic tan / white / light-gray necrotic center that gives leaf spot its 'white spot' / 'bird's-eye' common name; this is the most reliable field diagnostic. As lesions increase in number and size on heavily infected leaflets, multiple lesions coalesce into large, irregularly shaped, purplish-brown to brown necrotic areas covering 20-70% of the total leaflet area; at this stage, the entire leaflet and its petiole develop a general bright reddish-purple to purple-brown discoloration, the leaflet margins curl upward (inward, adaxially), giving the leaf a characteristic 'scorched', 'burned', or 'cupped' appearance (hence the disease name 'leaf scorch'), and the entire infected leaf will eventually die, turn dry brown, and abscise prematurely from the crown. Under humid, warm, dewy conditions, the asexual Marssonina anamorph stage produces microscopic, small, whitish-to-pale-brown, acervular fruiting bodies (acervuli 80-200 um diameter) in a ring-shaped pattern within the upper side of mature leaf scorch lesions; using a 20-40x compound microscope, one can observe characteristic two-celled (one septum near the center), hyaline to pale yellow, obovate to pear-shaped Marssonina conidia (18-30 x 5-8 um) that are typically slightly constricted at the septum, with a short 'beak' or 'pedicel' at the basal cell - this is diagnostic for D. earlianum / M. fragariae. In late summer and early autumn, after leaves begin senescing, the sexual Diplocarpon teleomorph stage produces small (100-250 um diameter), embedded, dark brown to black, apothecial ascigerous fruiting bodies within necrotic leaf blade and petiole tissue; each apothecium contains numerous club-shaped, 8-spored asci with elongated, 2-celled, fusoid-hyaline ascospores (18-28 x 4-7 um). In addition to leaf blades, D. earlianum also infects and produces lesions on strawberry petioles (elongated, slightly sunken, dark purple lesions 2-10 mm long that may girdle and kill the petiole), runners (runner blight - dark purple lesions that may kill the unrooted runner plant daughter plant), calyxes (fruit caps - purplish spots on the calyx leaves that reduce the cosmetic market quality of fresh-market strawberries), and very rarely on small green unripe strawberry fruit (small, dark purple superficial 'cap-end' lesions near the calyx, not usually of economic importance). D. earlianum overwinters primarily as immature apothecia and mycelium in infected dead strawberry leaf blades and petioles on the soil surface and within the crown of infected dormant strawberry plants; it also overwinters on infected perennial wild Fragaria vesca, F. virginiana, and F. chiloensis plants growing in field borders and hedgerows. In the following spring, approximately at the time of new strawberry leaf emergence and at the beginning of bloom, mature apothecia in overwintered leaf debris forcibly discharge ascospores into the air during periods of extended rainfall, heavy dew, or overhead sprinkler irrigation at temperatures of 10-22 C (optimum 15-18 C). Airborne ascospores are the primary source of inoculum for the first spring infections on the newly emerged trifoliate leaves. After the initial primary infections become established and produce the Marssonina anamorph acervuli, repeated polycyclic secondary cycles occur throughout the remainder of the growing season: conidia produced in acervuli are splash-dispersed by rain and overhead irrigation to new young leaflets; infection requires 6-24 hours of continuous free water on the leaf surface (optimum 12-18 hours) at temperatures of 12-26 C (optimum 20 C); the latent period (infection to visible new lesion with sporulating acervuli) is 9-16 days depending on temperature. Secondary splash-dispersed conidial cycles are repeated as long as conditions remain favorable (cool, moist weather, frequent dewy nights), and can cause devastating build-up of leaf scorch incidence from less than 1% of leaves infected at bloom to > 90% of leaves infected by harvest time, especially on highly susceptible cultivars. Severe leaf scorch epidemics are most severe on: (1) highly susceptible cultivars planted in heavily shaded, low-lying fields with poor air drainage; (2) strawberry plantings kept in production for more than 2-3 consecutive years in the same location (matted-row perennial systems); (3) fields watered with overhead sprinkler irrigation on a daily schedule rather than drip irrigation; (4) plantings with excessive nitrogen fertilization that promotes lush, overly succulent, weakly resistant foliage and delayed autumn dormancy. Management of strawberry leaf scorch follows an integrated multi-component program combining resistant cultivars, cultural practices, and judicious fungicide use. (1) Genetic resistance is the most effective and economical control measure. Two complementary types of resistance to D. earlianum are known in cultivated strawberries: (a) qualitative, monogenic, race-specific major R genes (Rde1, Rde2, Rde3, originally from F. virginiana subsp. glauca and F. chiloensis); these confer high-level hypersensitive resistance but have been overcome by new pathogenic races in several regions. (b) partial, horizontal, polygenic quantitative resistance (QTLs on Fragaria linkage groups FG2, FG4, FG6, FG7) conferring a reduction in lesion size, lesion number, and acervular sporulation rate; this is the durable preferred type of resistance for modern cultivars. The following commercially important cultivars have high to very high levels of quantitative partial leaf scorch resistance in Cornell, UMN, and AAFC (Canada) trials: 'Allstar' (one of the most scorch-resistant cultivars ever developed), 'Annapolis', 'Cavendish', 'Chambly', 'Darselect', 'Earliglow', 'Guardian', 'Honeoye' (moderate resistance), 'Jewel' (moderate), 'Kent', 'L'Amour', 'Mira', 'Northeaster', 'Primetime', 'Redchief', 'Sparkle', 'Surecrop', 'Tribute' (day-neutral; moderate), 'Tristar' (day-neutral; moderate). Highly susceptible cultivars (require intensive fungicide programs in wet years) include 'Benton', 'Blakemore', 'Catskill', 'Chandler', 'Dunlap', 'El Santa', 'Fort Laramie', 'Hecker', 'Olympus', 'Ozark Beauty', 'Pocahontas', 'Redgauntlet', 'Seneca', 'Shuksan', 'Tioga', 'Totem', 'Vesper'. (2) Cultural practices: (a) use wide (1.2-1.5 m), open row spacing and plant in fields with full sun exposure, good air movement, and good soil surface drainage; avoid shaded, low-lying, frost-pocket sites. (b) for matted-row perennial production systems in the Northeast and Midwest, renovate strawberry beds immediately after harvest each year by mowing off the old leaves to a height of 5 cm above the crowns, thinning plants to a 30 cm row width, removing all plant debris from the row, applying a light (50 kg/ha) nitrogen application, and irrigating to promote regrowth of a vigorous new canopy of healthy scorch-free foliage; annual post-harvest renovation alone reduces D. earlianum inoculum carry-over to the next season by 60-70%. (c) use annual hill plasticulture production systems (replanting fresh certified transplants every year on new raised beds with plastic mulch) instead of long-term matted-row perennial systems; this simple system change eliminates almost all overwintering inoculum within the field and reduces leaf scorch severity by 70-80% compared to multi-year matted-row fields on susceptible cultivars. (d) use drip tape irrigation under plastic mulch; AVOID overhead sprinkler irrigation entirely during the growing season unless absolutely necessary for establishment; if overhead irrigation must be used for frost protection, apply it early in the morning so the foliage dries completely within 4-6 hours after sunrise. (e) eliminate all perennial wild Fragaria weeds (F. vesca woodland strawberry, F. virginiana wild Virginia strawberry) from field borders, fencerows, irrigation ditches, and hedgerows within 500 m of the production field, as these serve as a perennial reservoir of both primary inoculum and new pathogenic races of D. earlianum. (f) avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization rates and late-autumn nitrogen applications which promote lush, highly susceptible late-season foliage and interfere with normal acclimation for winter dormancy. (g) at the end of the final production year (typically 2nd or 3rd year of a matted-row planting), completely remove, mow, chop, and incorporate all strawberry plants and leaf debris into the soil by moldboard plowing 15-20 cm deep immediately after the final harvest to destroy inoculum sources before the next crop. (3) Predictive forecasting models: the Strawberry Leaf Scorch Forecaster (UMD / Cornell) calculates daily leaf scorch infection risk values using 2 m air temperature, leaf wetness duration hours, relative humidity, and cultivar resistance rating; fungicide sprays are only scheduled when 3-day accumulated infection risk exceeds the cultivar-specific action threshold; forecasting typically reduces total seasonal leaf scorch fungicide use by 30-45% compared to calendar-based 14-day sprays while maintaining equivalent or better disease control. (4) Chemical fungicide programs for leaf scorch: in commercial production on susceptible cultivars, begin protectant fungicide applications at approximately 10% bloom (when the first newly emerged trifoliate leaves reach full size) and continue on 10-21 day intervals depending on disease pressure, rainfall, temperature, and forecasting model recommendations. The most effective FRAC groups against D. earlianum (Cornell, UMN, OMAFRA, and WSU trial data): FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, metconazole, prothioconazole, difenoconazole, tetraconazole, myclobutanil, fenbuconazole; excellent protectant + 3-4 day kickback curative activity; the DMI triazoles are consistently the most effective single-site chemical group for leaf scorch control across all regions). FRAC 11 QoI / strobilurins (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, picoxystrobin; good protectant + translaminar movement; QoI resistance in D. earlianum populations has been documented in a few isolated locations in Oregon, Spain, and British Columbia since 2018, so always tank-mix with multi-site and alternate with DMI and other groups). FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, boscalid, isofetamid, penthiopyrad; good protectant + mild systemic activity; SDHI + QoI or SDHI + DMI premixes are industry standard). FRAC M3 multi-site (captan, mancozeb, maneb, thiram; excellent zero-resistance-risk contact protectant; mandatory tank-mix partner for all single-site applications; captan is the preferred multi-site for strawberries due to superior crop safety). FRAC M1 copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, and Bordeaux mixture (moderate protectant; acceptable in organic programs under NOP rules; note: copper sprays on strawberry can cause fruit russeting under cool slow-drying conditions, so test copper products on a small block first). FRAC 9+12 cyprodinil + fludioxonil (Switch 62.5WG; moderate protectant activity against leaf scorch; excellent for combination programs targeting both leaf scorch and Botrytis gray mold simultaneously). Strict FRAC anti-resistance management: (i) always tank-mix every single-site application with full-rate captan or mancozeb. (ii) maximum 2 consecutive sprays of the same FRAC group. (iii) maximum 4-5 total seasonal applications of any single high-risk group (FRAC 11, FRAC 7). (iv) the first spray and the last spray of the season should each be a multi-site contact protectant (captan, mancozeb) to minimize resistance selection pressure. (5) Organic strawberry leaf scorch programs: combine resistant cultivars, annual hill plasticulture, drip irrigation, post-harvest renovation, and wild-fragaria eradication with 10-14 day rotational protectant sprays in the spring and autumn. Effective NOP-OMRI approved biorational products include: (a) micronized wettable sulfur (2-4 lb/100 gal) combined with a spreader-sticker; (b) fixed copper hydroxide / tribasic copper sulfate (1.5-2 lb/100 gal); (c) Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713 (Serenade ASO / Opti) + Reynoutria sachalinensis (Regalia Maxx) tank-mix; (d) Pseudomonas chlororaphis AFS009 (Howler) + Trichoderma asperellum / T. gamsii (Biotam 2.0 WP); (e) orange oil (Prev-Am Ultra, 0.5% v/v) + potassium bicarbonate (2 lb/100 gal). Well-designed organic programs achieve 45-70% leaf scorch reduction on susceptible cultivars in moderate disease years.
